newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss look to central bank to help boost growth.
newsitem.headline: Swiss look to central bank to help boost growth.

text.p: The Swiss Commission for Economic Issues said every sector of the economy must help make the country more competitive, and urged the Swiss National Bank (SNB) to use monetary policy to stimulate growth.
In a sober overview of economic trends, the commission -- part of the economics ministry -- said on Thursday there were no signs of a turnaround to a positive trend in the coming months.
"... all factors of influence must contribute to improving the relative competitive position," the commission said.
It said it could not tell when, or how strongly, the economy would return to growth and competitiveness begin to improve.
Noting Switzerland's comparatively high real interest rates, the Commission said it expected monetary policy "intensively to take advantage of the current scope."

The gloomy report was issued two days after the announcement that Swiss Gross Domestic Product (GDP) fell at an annual, seasonally-adjusted 0.9 percent in the second quarter from the first, the sixth quarterly decline in a row.

The continued weakness of the economy fuelled speculation the SNB might cut its symbolic discount rate. But the central bank's governing council left the discount rate unchanged at 1.5 percent at its weekly meeting today.

The report noted the expansion in the SNB's central money over the last few months was due partly to a change in the composition of banks' liquidity as they increased sight deposits at the SNB and reduced holdings in postal accounts.
"Monetary policy is thus less expansive than reflected by the central bank money supply," it said.

During the last few months the SNB has been generous in adding liquidity to Swiss money markets in light of rising money market rates and continued sluggish economic growth, which is helping keep inflation under control.
Higher liquidity has held down money market rates and offset some of the Swiss franc's recent gains, which make Swiss exports less competitive.

The commission noted that some of the conditions for economic improvement were in place: Prices remain stable, nominal interest rates are relatively low and the global economy is improving, including the German economy.

"Nevertheless, we cannot point to any significant reduction in the high external value of the Swiss franc. Overall the uncertainties are great regarding the exact time of an economic turnaround and the strength of it," the commission said.
The competitive position of Switzerland has deteriorated over the last five years and the high value of the Swiss franc and rising unit wage costs have contributed to this.
"Improvements require a significant growth in Europe's economy and a lower external value of the franc," it added.
The commission said more flexible working conditions and a differentiation in the wage structure would benefit economic growth.
